newsitem.title: USA: Brazil lays out domestic debt, privatization plan.
newsitem.headline: Brazil lays out domestic debt, privatization plan.

text.p: Under the gaze of world policymakers and investors, Brazil outlined this week a commitment to restructure its debt burden and sell off state firms in hopes of building more sustainable growth.

Brazilian officials, who travelled here to attend the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings, mapped out a strategy to replace their costly domestic debt with revenues from privatization and borrowings on the international capital markets.
On Sunday, Brazil announced that it would issue about $750 million of 5- or 10-year Yankee bonds, and use the proceeds to retire domestic debt.

Brazilian Central Bank President Gustavo Loyola told Reuters on Monday the government sought to use the foreign markets to capital to pay down local currency paper, and that future such transactions would depend on market conditions.
"The idea is not to replace all the (domestic) debt, but just part of it," Loyola said. "It depends on market conditions, but it's a decision we're taking on a case-by-case basis."

The Yankee issue, which surprised many market observers, would be Brazil's first offering on the prestigious U.S. bond market, and Loyola said the potential for future such bonds would depend on market conditions.

Brazil's domestic debt has swelled over the past year, as international capital has flowed into the country, and the central bank was forced to "sterilize" the dollars, or prevent them from expanding the money supply, by selling real-denominated debt.

Two years into its Real plan that stabilized the economy from an era of hyperinflation, the most serious challenge to the Brazilian economic outlook comes from the high fiscal deficit, officials said.

The government's operational deficit in 1996 would likely be 3.0- 3.5 percent of GDP, down from five percent last year, according Finance Minister Pedro Malan. He added that it was "too early" to tell whether the figures would need to be revised higher.
The finance minister also said said Monday that Brazil needs to move forward on privatization and reducing public sector spending to build sustainable growth with low inflation.
"To consolidate the gains we've had so far, we need to push forward on privatization and reduction of the consolidated public debt," Malan said. "That's precisely what we intend to do."

Planning Minister Antonio Kandir told a conference that Brazil planned a heavy scheduled of privatizations next year, including the sell-off of mining giant CVRD, and final sales of the railways and the energy company Light.
He said that the proceeds of privatizations, amounting to 8-10 million reias would be "considerably reduce the consolidated public deficit."
Malan said Sunday that he expected the country's total public sector debt would stabilize around 35-36 percent of GDP, compared with current levels of 34.7 percent of GDP.
Improvement on the fiscal front would enable the central bank to ease the reins on monetary policy, Loyola said.
"I am convinced that as the deindexation deepens and the fiscal situation improves, there will be room for further interest rate reductions," Loyola said.
"In the future rates will be even lower, it depends o developments in the developments on the macroeconomic side.
